title: 04. BM25 & Lexical Search: What is an Inverted Index?
summary: Open any textbook and flip to the very last pages. You'll find an index like this: > > > > It maps words → page numbers.

sections.title: ① Real-World Analogy
sections.body:
> Open any **textbook** and flip to the very last pages. You'll find an **index** like this:
>
> ```
> Algorithm ............. 45, 67, 123, 201
> Binary tree ........... 89, 90, 91
> Cache ................. 34, 201, 345
> ```
>
> It maps **words → page numbers**. That's exactly an inverted index.
>
> Now imagine doing this for **every word in every book in a library of 1 million books**. That's what a search engine builds — one giant book index for all documents combined.
>
> It's called "inverted" because normally you think of a document as containing words. Here we *invert* that: we map **words → documents**.

sections.title: ② Plain English Explanation
sections.body:
An inverted index is a dictionary where:
- **Keys** = every unique word across all documents
- **Values** = a list of documents (and positions) where that word appears

When you search for a word, you simply look it up in this dictionary. Instead of scanning millions of documents, you get the answer in one lookup — like looking up a word in a dictionary.

The list of documents for each word is called a **posting list**.

sections.title: ③ Why Does This Matter?
sections.body:
Without an inverted index, searching 1 billion webpages would take hours. With it, it takes milliseconds. This is *the* fundamental data structure that makes Google, Elasticsearch, and every search engine work.

It also enables complex queries — searching for documents that contain word A AND word B is just finding the intersection of two posting lists.

sections.title: ④ Step-by-Step Technical Explanation
sections.body:
**Our 5 documents (we'll use these ALL the way through):**
```
Doc 0: "Python is great for machine learning and data science"
Doc 1: "Java is used for enterprise software development"
Doc 2: "Python and Java are both popular programming languages"
Doc 3: "Machine learning requires lots of data and computation"
Doc 4: "Data science uses Python for statistical analysis and modeling"
```

**Step 1: Process Doc 0**
Words: python, is, great, for, machine, learning, and, data, science
→ Add each word to the index, pointing to Doc 0

**Step 2: Process Doc 1**
Words: java, is, used, for, enterprise, software, development
→ "is" and "for" already in index — add Doc 1 to their posting lists

**Step 3: Continue for all docs...**

**Resulting index (excerpt):**
```
Word         | Posting List (Doc IDs)
-------------|------------------------
"python"     | [0, 2, 4]
"java"       | [1, 2]
"is"         | [0, 1]
"machine"    | [0, 3]
"learning"   | [0, 3]
"data"       | [0, 3, 4]
"science"    | [0, 4]
"enterprise" | [1]
```

sections.title: ⑤ Beginner-Friendly Code Example
sections.body:
```python
# ============================================================
# LESSON 2: Building an Inverted Index from Scratch
# ============================================================

import string  # We'll use this to remove punctuation

# Our 5 documents — these are the SAME documents we'll use in every lesson
documents = [
    "Python is great for machine learning and data science",        # Doc 0
    "Java is used for enterprise software development",              # Doc 1
    "Python and Java are both popular programming languages",        # Doc 2
    "Machine learning requires lots of data and computation",        # Doc 3
    "Data science uses Python for statistical analysis and modeling" # Doc 4
]

# ── STEP 1: Tokenisation ──────────────────────────────────────────────

def tokenise(text):
    """
    Convert a string of text into a list of clean word tokens.
    'Clean' means: lowercase + no punctuation
    """
    # Make everything lowercase: "Python" → "python"
    text = text.lower()
    
    # Remove punctuation: "hello," → "hello"
    # str.maketrans creates a translation table that maps each punctuation char to None
    text = text.translate(str.maketrans('', '', string.punctuation))
    
    # Split on whitespace: "hello world" → ["hello", "world"]
    tokens = text.split()
    
    return tokens

# Test our tokeniser
print("=== Testing Tokeniser ===")
test_text = "Python is Great, isn't it?"
print(f"Input:  '{test_text}'")
print(f"Output: {tokenise(test_text)}")
print()

# ── STEP 2: Tokenise All Documents ────────────────────────────────────

print("=== Tokenised Documents ===")
tokenised_docs = []
for i, doc in enumerate(documents):
    tokens = tokenise(doc)
    tokenised_docs.append(tokens)
    print(f"Doc {i}: {tokens}")
print()

# ── STEP 3: Build the Inverted Index ──────────────────────────────────

# The inverted index: maps each word to the docs it appears in
# We'll also store the COUNT (how many times it appears in each doc)
# Structure: { word: { doc_id: count, doc_id: count, ... } }

inverted_index = {}

for doc_id, tokens in enumerate(tokenised_docs):
    for word in tokens:
        # If this is the first time we've seen this word, initialise it
        if word not in inverted_index:
            inverted_index[word] = {}
        
        # Increment the count of this word in this document
        # .get(doc_id, 0) means: get current count, or 0 if not set yet
        current_count = inverted_index[word].get(doc_id, 0)
        inverted_index[word][doc_id] = current_count + 1

# ── STEP 4: Print the Index ───────────────────────────────────────────

print("=== Full Inverted Index ===")
print(f"{'Word':<15} | {'Posting List (doc_id: count)'}")
print("-" * 55)
for word, posting_list in sorted(inverted_index.items()):
    print(f"'{word}':{'':<{12-len(word)}} | {posting_list}")

print()

# ── STEP 5: Simple Lookup ─────────────────────────────────────────────

def lookup(word, inverted_index, documents):
    """Find all documents containing a specific word"""
    word = word.lower()  # Make sure query is also lowercase
    
    if word not in inverted_index:
        print(f"Word '{word}' not found in any document!")
        return
    
    posting_list = inverted_index[word]
    print(f"Word '{word}' found in {len(posting_list)} document(s):")
    
    for doc_id, count in posting_list.items():
        print(f"  → Doc {doc_id} (appears {count} time(s)): '{documents[doc_id]}'")

# Test lookups
print("=== Lookups ===")
lookup("python", inverted_index, documents)
print()
lookup("data", inverted_index, documents)
print()
lookup("quantum", inverted_index, documents)  # This word doesn't exist!
print()

# ── STEP 6: AND Search (must contain BOTH words) ──────────────────────

def and_search(word1, word2, inverted_index, documents):
    """
    Find documents that contain BOTH word1 AND word2.
    This is just finding the intersection of two posting lists!
    """
    word1, word2 = word1.lower(), word2.lower()
    
    # Get doc IDs for each word
    docs_with_word1 = set(inverted_index.get(word1, {}).keys())
    docs_with_word2 = set(inverted_index.get(word2, {}).keys())
    
    # Intersection: only docs that appear in BOTH lists
    both_docs = docs_with_word1 & docs_with_word2
    
    print(f"Docs with '{word1}': {docs_with_word1}")
    print(f"Docs with '{word2}': {docs_with_word2}")
    print(f"Docs with BOTH:     {both_docs}")
    
    for doc_id in both_docs:
        print(f"  → Doc {doc_id}: '{documents[doc_id]}'")

print("=== AND Search: 'python' AND 'data' ===")
and_search("python", "data", inverted_index, documents)
```

**Expected Output:**
```
=== Testing Tokeniser ===
Input:  'Python is Great, isn't it?'
Output: ['python', 'is', 'great', 'isnt', 'it']

=== Tokenised Documents ===
Doc 0: ['python', 'is', 'great', 'for', 'machine', 'learning', 'and', 'data', 'science']
Doc 1: ['java', 'is', 'used', 'for', 'enterprise', 'software', 'development']
Doc 2: ['python', 'and', 'java', 'are', 'both', 'popular', 'programming', 'languages']
Doc 3: ['machine', 'learning', 'requires', 'lots', 'of', 'data', 'and', 'computation']
Doc 4: ['data', 'science', 'uses', 'python', 'for', 'statistical', 'analysis', 'and', 'modeling']

=== Full Inverted Index ===
Word            | Posting List (doc_id: count)
-------------------------------------------------------
'analysis':     | {4: 1}
'and':          | {0: 1, 2: 1, 3: 1, 4: 1}
'are':          | {2: 1}
'both':         | {2: 1}
'computation':  | {3: 1}
'data':         | {0: 1, 3: 1, 4: 1}
'development':  | {1: 1}
'enterprise':   | {1: 1}
'for':          | {0: 1, 1: 1, 4: 1}
'great':        | {0: 1}
'is':           | {0: 1, 1: 1}
'java':         | {1: 1, 2: 1}
'languages':    | {2: 1}
'learning':     | {0: 1, 3: 1}
'lots':         | {3: 1}
'machine':      | {0: 1, 3: 1}
'modeling':     | {4: 1}
'of':           | {3: 1}
'popular':      | {2: 1}
'programming':  | {2: 1}
'python':       | {0: 1, 2: 1, 4: 1}
'requires':     | {3: 1}
'science':      | {0: 1, 4: 1}
'software':     | {1: 1}
'statistical':  | {4: 1}
'used':         | {1: 1}
'uses':         | {4: 1}

=== Lookups ===
Word 'python' found in 3 document(s):
  → Doc 0 (appears 1 time(s)): 'Python is great for machine learning and data science'
  → Doc 2 (appears 1 time(s)): 'Python and Java are both popular programming languages'
  → Doc 4 (appears 1 time(s)): 'Data science uses Python for statistical analysis and modeling'

Word 'data' found in 3 document(s):
  → Doc 0 (appears 1 time(s)): 'Python is great for machine learning and data science'
  → Doc 3 (appears 1 time(s)): 'Machine learning requires lots of data and computation'
  → Doc 4 (appears 1 time(s)): 'Data science uses Python for statistical analysis and modeling'

Word 'quantum' not found in any document!

=== AND Search: 'python' AND 'data' ===
Docs with 'python': {0, 2, 4}
Docs with 'data': {0, 3, 4}
Docs with BOTH:     {0, 4}
```

sections.title: ⑥ Common Beginner Mistakes
sections.body:
❌ **Mistake 1:** Not lowercasing — "Python" and "python" create two separate index entries
✅ **Fix:** Always `.lower()` both documents and queries

❌ **Mistake 2:** Forgetting punctuation removal — "science," and "science" are treated as different words
✅ **Fix:** Strip punctuation using `str.translate(str.maketrans('', '', string.punctuation))`

❌ **Mistake 3:** Rebuilding the index on every search
✅ **Fix:** Build the index once, store it, reuse it for all searches

❌ **Mistake 4:** Storing only doc IDs, not counts — you lose frequency information needed for scoring
✅ **Fix:** Store `{doc_id: count}` in each posting list

❌ **Mistake 5:** Thinking "inverted" means upside-down or reversed
✅ **Fix:** "Inverted" means the mapping direction is flipped: normally doc→words, here it's word→docs

sections.title: ⑦ Quick Recap
sections.body:
- 📖 An inverted index maps **words → documents** (the "inverted" direction vs normal doc→words)
- 📋 Each word has a **posting list**: the list of documents containing that word
- ⚡ Lookup is **O(1)** — instant — regardless of how many documents you have
- 🔢 We store **counts** in the posting list, not just doc IDs — needed for scoring later
- 🔗 AND/OR queries = set intersection/union of posting lists

sections.title: ⑧ Visual Explanation
sections.body:
```
╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║                     INVERTED INDEX — HOW IT WORKS                   ║
╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝

 DOCUMENTS (normal direction: doc → words)
 ═══════════════════════════════════════════

 Doc 0  ──▶  [python, is, great, for, machine, learning, and, data, science]
 Doc 1  ──▶  [java, is, used, for, enterprise, software, development]
 Doc 2  ──▶  [python, and, java, are, both, popular, programming, languages]
 Doc 3  ──▶  [machine, learning, requires, lots, of, data, and, computation]
 Doc 4  ──▶  [data, science, uses, python, for, statistical, analysis, modeling]

 INVERTED INDEX (inverted direction: word → docs)
 ══════════════════════════════════════════════════

 "python"    ──▶  ┌──────────────────────────┐
                  │  Doc0(×1)  Doc2(×1)  Doc4(×1) │  ← POSTING LIST
                  └──────────────────────────┘

 "java"      ──▶  ┌──────────────────┐
                  │  Doc1(×1)  Doc2(×1) │
                  └──────────────────┘

 "machine"   ──▶  ┌──────────────────┐
                  │  Doc0(×1)  Doc3(×1) │
                  └──────────────────┘

 "data"      ──▶  ┌──────────────────────────┐
                  │  Doc0(×1)  Doc3(×1)  Doc4(×1) │
                  └──────────────────────────┘

 "enterprise"──▶  ┌─────────┐
                  │  Doc1(×1) │   ← Only 1 doc! (rare word)
                  └─────────┘

 HOW A SEARCH WORKS
 ═══════════════════

 Query: "python data"
          │
          ├─ "python" → {Doc0, Doc2, Doc4}
          │
          ├─ "data"   → {Doc0, Doc3, Doc4}
          │
          └─ UNION    → {Doc0: 2pts, Doc2: 1pt, Doc3: 1pt, Doc4: 2pts}
                                 ↑                                 ↑
                           (matched 2 words)                (matched 2 words)

 RANKED RESULTS: Doc0 ≥ Doc4 > Doc2 = Doc3

 ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
 Why "INVERTED"? Normal = Doc→Words. Inverted = Words→Docs
 ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
```
